parole.significato: forms adjectives that denote where something or someone is from
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -ois, from Old French -eis (feminine form -esche). In some senses from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin -iscus (from Frankish *-isk, from Proto-Germanic *-iskaz (“-ish”), conflated with Ancient Greek -ισκος (-iskos), all ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos), in others fr
Inherited from Middle French -esse, from Old French -esse, from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa).
Inherited from Middle French -et, from Old French -et, from Late Latin -ittus (whence Spanish -ito).

parole.significato: forms colloquial nouns, chiefly with hypocoristic effect
parole.testo: Apparently originally a dialectal reflex of Late Latin -icia, a suffix used to create abstract nouns from adjectives, from Latin -itia.
From Old French -iser, from earlier -izer, borrowed from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -oyer, which was inherited.
From Late Latin latria, from Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service; worship”).

parole.significato: a suffix used to form some verbs, often with factitive effect
parole.testo: From Old French -oiier, inherited from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -iser, which was borrowed.
From Late Latin sphēra, earlier Latin sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: to butcher; to slaughter for meat
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French abbatre, from Old French abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere. Cognate with Catalan abatre, Corsican abbatta, abbatte, Galician abater, Italian abbattere, Occitan abatre, Portuguese abater, Romanian abate, Sardinian abbàttiri, Sicilian abbàttiri, Spanish
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abbātiāl|is, ~e (“abbatial”).
Inherited from Middle French abbaïe, from Old French abaïe, from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin abbatia.
Borrowed from Late Latin abdicātīvus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin abōminābilis (“abominable, detestable”).

parole.significato: something vile and abominable; an abomination
parole.testo: From Late Latin abōminātiōnem.

parole.significato: a shelter or refuge against the elements or physical danger
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French abri, from Old French abri (“a place where one is sheltered from the elements or harm”), from abrier (“to cover”), from Late Latin abrigō (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + brigō, from Frankish *biwrīhan (“to cover, protect”), from Frankish *bi- (“be-”) + *wrīhan, from Pro
Inherited from Old French abregier, itself from Late Latin abbreviāre. Doublet of abrévier, a (now obsolete) borrowing. See also abréviation.
Borrowed from Late Latin abstentiōnem, from Latin abstentus, from abstineō.
Borrowed from Late Latin abstrāctiōnem.
From Middle French abyssal (16th c.), from Late Latin abyssālis. By surface analysis, abysse + -al, though the noun is younger in French than the adjective.
From abime, abîme, from Late Latin *abyssimus < Latin abyssus (“abyss”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless pit”).
Borrowed from Late Latin accessibilis (“accessible”), from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”).
Inherited from Late Latin accubitāre, with the influence of Old French acoster.

Inherited from Old French acier, acer, from Late Latin aciārium, from Latin acies, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Compare Catalan acer, Galician aceiro, Italian acciaio, Occitan acièr, Portuguese aço, Spanish acero.
Borrowed from Late Latin acuitātem.

parole.significato: the moral of a fable, tale, story, etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin affābulātiō. By surface analysis, affabuler + -tion.
Inherited from Old French aguille, from Late Latin acūcula, diminutive of Latin acus (“needle”). Perhaps influenced phonetically by aiguiser. Compare Occitan agulha.

As with lisser, one suggested origin is a cross of Late Latin lixare and allisus. TLFi asserts that derivation from Spanish alisio (“trade (wind)”) is impossible and argues the Spanish word more likely derives from French.
Inherited from Old French alaitier, from Late Latin allactāre, derived from Latin lac (“milk”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + lait + -er.
Inherited from Late Latin alleviāre.
From Late Latin alosa, alausa, from Gaulish *alausa.

parole.significato: alphabet (set of letters considered as a group)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha) (Α,α) and βῆτα (bêta) (Β,β) (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician aleph 𐤀 (ʾ, “ox”) and beth 𐤁 (b, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects, having deve
From Old French amiable, from Late Latin amīcābilis.

Inherited from Old French ameillorer, from a prefixed version of Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”). The modern French form was modified under Latin influence, hence the otherwise-unexpected /lj/ (instead of /j/ < /ʎ/).
Borrowed from Late Latin anacolūthon, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνακόλουθον (anakólouthon).

Inherited from Old French ancestrel, from ancestre (“ancestor”), from Late Latin antecessor, an agent noun from the past participle stem of Latin antecedere (“to proceed”), from the prefix ante- with the infinitive cedere (“to go”), the latter from Proto-Italic *kezdō (“to avoid or to go away”), fro

parole.significato: angary (the right of a belligerent to seize property belonging to other nations or to take over ships during a war)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin angaria (“forced service”).
Inherited from Old French ange, angle, from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Doublet of angélus.

parole.significato: to annihilate (to reduce to nothing, to destroy, to eradicate)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin annihilāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin annuālis, from Latin annus (“year”).
Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis). By surface analysis, anti- + phrasis.
Borrowed from Late Latin antipodes, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + πόδες (pódes), nominative plural of πούς (poús, “foot”).

Via Late Latin apophasis from Ancient Greek ἀπόφασις (apóphasis, “denial, negation”) from ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + φάσις (phásis, “statement, proposition”) from φημί (phēmí, “to speak”) from Proto-Hellenic *pʰā́mā from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂; whence Latin fārī, cognate to English fame, f
Borrowed from Late Latin apoplexia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostolātus. See apôtre and -at.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin apothecārius. Compare French boutiquier.
Inherited from Middle French apparoistre, from Old French aparoistre, from Late Latin appārēscere (“begin to appear”), from Latin appareō.
Inherited from Old French apartenir, borrowed from Late Latin appertinēre (“belong to”), from Latin pertineō. Cf. also Old French partenir.
From the Late Latin appellātīvus.

Deverbal of appointer. from Old French apoint (“favorable occasion; resolution, agreement”), from Old French apointier (“to work out, solve”), from Late Latin appunctare (“to bring back to the point, restore, to fix the point in a controversy, or the points in an agreement”); Latin ad + punctum (“a

parole.significato: to salary (attribute a salary to a position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French apointier. By surface analysis, a- + point + -er. Possibly corresponds to a Late Latin appunctāre, from Latin ad + punctum.

parole.significato: to approach, to come close to, to move towards
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French aprochier, from Late Latin appropiāre, a verb based on Latin prope (“near”).
Borrowed from Late Latin appropriāre, from Latin proprius. See a-, propre and -er.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin appretiāre (“to appraise”), from Latin pretium. Cf. also the Old French aprisier.
Inherited from Middle French aprés, from Old French aprés, from Late Latin ad pressum, from Latin ad + pressum. Compare obsolete Spanish aprés.
Inherited from Old French apostre (c. 1180), apostle (c. 1100), borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “one sent forth, apostle”).
Inherited from Old French arbaleste, from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”) + ballista (“ballista”).
Borrowed from Late Latin archaicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊκός (arkhaïkós).
Inherited from Old French arche, borrowed from Late Latin arca, from Latin arcus.

Inherited from Old French archevesque, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “first, chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”), from ἐπισκοπέω (episkopéō, “to watch over”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”), + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to examine”).
Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin archidiaconus. Equivalent to archi- + diacre.

From vernacular Late Latin of Northern France like Vulgar Latin *ardēsia, possibly from Gaulish artuā or Gaulish root *ard(u)- (“high, in altitude”), found also in Ardu-enna (the Ardennes), a region where slate has been quarried for centuries.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin argumentātor.

Inherited from Middle French arme, from Old French arme, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).
Inherited from Old French aromatique.
Inherited from Late Latin arepennis (“surface of a field”), from Gaulish *are-penno- (“end, extremity of a field”).
From Late Latin artista.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).

parole.significato: to assail; to assault; to attack
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre (“attack”, literally “jump on”), from Latin salīre (“jump”).

parole.significato: to a sufficient or moderate degree; enough; sufficiently
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French assez, from Old French asez, from Late Latin ad satis, from Latin ad + satis. Cognate with Franco-Provençal asséds, Occitan assatz, Italian assai, Portuguese assaz, and Spanish asaz. Doublet of assai.
Borrowed from Late Latin assistentia.
From Late Latin astrālis, from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).
From Late Latin astrologicus, from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, astrologie + -ique.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages”), diminutive of ἀστήρ (astḗr, “a star”); see Latin aster.
Inherited from Late Latin astella, from astla, from Latin assula (“splinter”).
Borrowed from Late Latin attractīvus.
Inherited from Old French aube espine, from Late Latin alba spīna, from Latin alba (“white”) + spīna (“thorn”). Cf. Italian albaspina, Catalan albespí.
Borrowed from Late Latin audibilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin augmentātiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin augmentāre (“increase”), from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”).
From Old French aumosnier, itself inherited from Late Latin eleemosynārius.
Inherited from Old French (h)ostur, from Late Latin auceptor, from accipiter.
Inherited from Middle French avant, from Old French avant (“before, prior in time, forward”), from Late Latin ab ante (“before, in front of”), from Latin ab (“from”) + ante (“before”).
Inherited from Late Latin aviola, diminutive from Latin avia. Feminine counterpart to aïeul.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain; probably from Late Latin baia, ultimately from Iberian.
Inherited from Late Latin baiula, from the feminine of baiulus.
Inherited from Old French bal, deverbal of baller, from Late Latin ballare (“to dance”).

Inherited from Middle French baller, from Old French baller, baler, from Late Latin ballāre (“to dance”), itself borrowed from, or related to, Ancient Greek βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Cognate with Catalan ballar, Italian ballare, Portuguese bailar, Spanish bailar.
From Late Latin balsaminus, from Latin balsamum.

Borrowed from Late Latin benna (“wicker carriage”), related to benne used in Norman and Lyonnais. The meaning of bâche (“covering, tarp”) is the same that connects bâche and basket, see also Latin bascauda.

parole.significato: to trumpet (to make the sound of an elephant's cry)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French barrire, from Late Latin barriō (“to make the sound of an elephant”), from Latin barrus (“elephant”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin barytŏnus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βαρύτονος (barútonos).
Inherited from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus.
From Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”), from Egyptian.
Inherited from Middle French bataille, from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō, of Gaulish origin.
Inherited from Old French beneoit, inherited from Late Latin benedictus, from Latin benedīcō. Doublet of bénit, béni, and benêt.
Inherited from Old French bergier, from Late Latin vervēcārius, from vervēx + -ārius. Compare Romanian berbecar, Piedmontese bërgé, Sardinian berbecarju, berbecàlgiu, berbegarzu.
Borrowed from Late Latin bēstiālis, from Latin bēstia (“beast”).
From bienfait + -eur, modeled on Late Latin benefactōrem (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin benefaciō (“benefit someone”), from bene (“good”) + faciō (“do, make”).

parole.significato: biotic (relating to or produced by life or living organisms)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin bioticus, from Ancient Greek βιωτικός (biōtikós), from βίος (bíos, “life”).
Inherited from Old French besistre, Late Latin bisextus (“intercalary day”); so called because intercalary days were seen as portending misery.
From Old French blasfemer, which was borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmāre. Doublet of blâmer, which was inherited.

Inherited from Middle French bleu, from Old French blöe, bleve, blef, bleu (“blue”), from Late Latin blāvus, from Frankish *blāu (“blue”), from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰléh₁-, *bʰlh₁-, *bʰleh₁- (“yellow, grey, blue”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shine”).
Inherited from Old French blasmer, from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasphémer, which was borrowed from Latin.

parole.significato: act of drinking, consumption of a liquid
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bibitiōnem, from Latin bibitus, from bibere (“to drink”).
Inherited from Middle French bol, from Old French bol, borrowed from Late Latin bōlus (“clod of earth, lump”), from Ancient Greek βῶλος (bôlos, “clod, lump”).
Inherited from Middle French bombasin (m), in the feminine form; Late Latin bombasinum, ultimately from bombyx (“silkworm”).
Inherited from Old French bouge, bolge (“sack, purse”), probably borrowed from Late Latin bulga, from Gaulish bolgā (“bag, sack”).

From Old French bogre (“heretic”) (1172), also bogresse (“person who indulges in unnatural debauchery”) (1260), from Late Latin Bulgarus (“Bulgarian”), from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ). Doublet of bulgare and boug.
Inherited from Middle French bourgois, from Old French borgeis (“town dweller”), from Late Latin burgensis. By surface analysis, bourg + -ois.
Inherited from Old French boure, borre, from Late Latin burra (“coarse fabric or material”).

parole.significato: bottle (container, typically made of glass or plastic and having a tapered neck, used primarily for holding liquids)
parole.testo: From Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula.
Borrowed from Late Latin bovinus.
Inherited from Old French branche, from Late Latin branca, possibly of Gaulish origin.
Inherited from Old French bretesche, from Late Latin brittisca.

Inherited from Middle French briser, from Old French brisier (“to break to pieces by a shock or violent blow, bust”), from Late Latin brisāre, of uncertain further origin. Possibly of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bristijan, *bristan, *brestan (“to burst, break, split, shatter”), from Proto-German

Inherited from Middle French brouet, from Old French broet, diminutive of Old French breu, *brou, from Late Latin brodium, from Frankish *broþ, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“broth”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to seethe, brew”). Cognate with English broth, Icelandic broð.

From Middle French bru, from Old French bru, brui, bruz, from Late Latin bruta, brutis, from Old High German brūt (“daughter-in-law, bride”) or Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌸𐍃 (bruþs, “daughter-in-law”); both from Proto-Germanic *brūdiz (“bride, daughter-in-law”). Akin to Old English brȳd (“bride”), English bride.
From Late Latin butomus.
From Late Latin byzantinus itself from Byzantium.

parole.significato: retrognathous (of the teeth of a horse etc.)
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps derived in some way from Late Latin beccus (“beak”), in which case related to bec.
From Middle French bêche, besche, from Old French besche, from Late Latin besca, bescia, from Frankish *bikkju (“pickaxe, spade”).

parole.significato: to baa; to bleat (make cry of sheep)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bēlāre, a variant of bālō.

parole.significato: beast of burden (animal that carries or pulls heavy loads)
parole.testo: bête + de + somme (“pack, packsaddle”), which is from Late Latin sauma, from Latin sagma (“packsaddle”).
From the Médoc dialect of southwestern France, but of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly from Late Latin caput nigrum (“black vine”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cachexia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek καχεξία (kakhexía).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin calumniōsus. By surface analysis, calomnie + -eux.
Borrowed from Late Latin cambium.

Inherited from Middle French capitaine, from Old French capitaine, borrowed from Late Latin capitaneus, from Latin caput. Compare the inherited Old French chevetaine (whence English chieftain). Doublet of cheftaine.
Inherited from Old French capote (“hooded cloak”), diminutive of cape, from Late Latin cappa. Piecewise doublet of capote.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin captiōsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin carentia, from Latin careō (“to lack”).

parole.significato: carillon (set of bells, often in a bell tower)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French quarrillon, from Late Latin quaterniōnem, from quaterniō (“group of four things”).
From Late Latin carpa, probably from a language of eastern Europe.

Borrowed from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register, a list, catalogue”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length or in order, to make a list”), from κατα- (kata-, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, to pick up, t
Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρᾱ (kathédrā, “seat”).
Inherited from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria.
Borrowed from Late Latin causālis, from Latin causa.
From Late Latin cauterizāre, from Ancient Greek καυτηριάζω (kautēriázō).
Borrowed from Late Latin cava, substantivized form of Latin cava, feminine of the adjective cavus.
Inherited from Old French ço, from Late Latin ecce hoc.
Inherited from Old French celier, from Late Latin cellārium (“pantry”), from Latin cella.
From Middle French certitude, borrowed from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus (“sure”).

parole.significato: oxy-fuel torch (usually oxy-acetylene; used for cutting, welding, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French chalemel, from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”). Doublet of caramel.

Inherited from Middle French chamois, from Late Latin camox, from Gaulish camox (5th c. AD, Polemius Silvius), probably from an extinct Alpine language (Raetic, Ancient Ligurian), possibly Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“without horns”).

parole.significato: champagne (“wine from the Champagne region of France”)
parole.testo: From the region Champagne, from Late Latin campānia (in this case, Campania Remensis specifically), from campāneus, from Latin campus.

parole.significato: an expanse of flat and open cultivated earth
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French champagne, champaigne, from Late Latin campānia, from campāneus, from Latin campus. Compare Occitan campanha, Catalan campanya, Italian campagna, Spanish campaña, Portuguese campanha. Doublet of campagne.
From Old French chancelier, cancelier, from inherited from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus.

Inherited from Old French chanvre, chenvre, inherited from Late Latin canava, canapus, altered form of the Classical Latin cannabis, a borrowing from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of cannabis, which was a later borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Old French chape, from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of cape.

parole.significato: a circus tent, or any similar set-up used for spectacles or events
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French chapitel, from Late Latin capitellum (likely a semi-learned borrowing), from Latin capitulum, ultimately from caput (“head”), whence also French chef. Doublet of cadeau and cadet, borrowings from Occitan, and caudillo, a borrowing from Spanish.

From Middle French chapitre, from Old French chapitre (also capitre, chapitle), an early borrowing from Late Latin capitulum (literally “little head”), diminutive of Latin caput (whence French chef). If inherited through Vulgar Latin, it would have yielded *cheveil. Doublet of capitule, a modern bor
Probably ultimately from a derivative of Late Latin cardella, cardellus, from Latin carduelis, from carduus. Compare Italian cardellino, cardello, cardelletto, Romanian căldăraș, Spanish cardelina.
Inherited from Old French chargier, from Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”). Compare Spanish cargar.

parole.significato: charivari, shivaree (mock serenade of discordant noise, notably to heckle a publicly reviled figure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French chalivali (“noise from pots and pans”), from Late Latin caribaria, from carivaria, from Ancient Greek καρηβάρεια (karēbáreia, “headache”, from κάρη (kárē, “head”) + βαρύς (barús, “heavy”)).
From Old French charpantier, carpentier, from Late Latin carpentārius (“carpenter”), from Latin carpentārius (“wagon-maker, carriage-maker”).
From Old French chesible, from Late Latin casubla, an alteration of Latin casula (“little cottage, hooded cloak”), a diminutive of casa (“house”).
Inherited from Middle French chat, from Old French chat, from Late Latin cattus.
Alteration (after chat, huant) of Zarphatic Old French javan (“owl”), from Old French choan, from Late Latin cavannus, from Transalpine Gaulish.
Inherited from Middle French chatte, from Old French chate, from Late Latin catta, feminine of cattus. By surface analysis, chat + -e.
Inherited from Old French chaudiere, from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).
Inherited from Middle French chaudron, from Old French chauderon, ultimately from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”). Compare English cauldron (from the northern Old French variant caudron).

parole.significato: bat (a small flying mammal of the order Chiroptera)
parole.testo: Used as early as the 8th century in Gallic Late Latin calva sōrex (“bald mouse”); the first element ("bald") may originally be an alteration of Vulgar Latin *cawa (“crow, tawny owl”). Equivalent to chauve (“bald”) + souris (“mouse”). Compare Late Latin mūs caecus (“bat”, literally “blind mouse”).
From Old French cheminee, from Late Latin [camera] camīnāta, from Latin camīnus (“furnace”), from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos). Unrelated to cheminer or chemin although an influence is possible.
Inherited from Old French chemise, from Late Latin camisia, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”).
Inherited from Old French chenu, inherited from Late Latin cānūtus, from Latin cānus.
Inherited from Middle French chercher, cercher, altered from Old French cerchier through assimilation, from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.
Inherited from Middle French chevalier, from Old French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Doublet of cavalier.
Inherited from Middle French chevauchier, from Old French chevauchier, from Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus (“nag, jade”).
Inherited from Middle French cheoir, from Old French cheoir, from older chedeir, from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre, from Proto-Italic *kadō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱh₂d- (“to fall”).
Borrowed from Late Latin cholera, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ). Doublet of colère.
Borrowed from Late Latin chorion.
Borrowed from Late Latin Christiānismus, from Ancient Greek Χριστιανός (Khristianós), from Χριστός (Khristós, “Christ, anointed one”).
From Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma, “anointing”, “unction”), from χρίω (khríō, “anoint”).
From Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Inherited from Old French chasse, from Late Latin capsa, from Classical Latin capsus, whence also the doublets casse and caisse.

Inherited from Middle French chenevis, cheneveux, from Old French chenevuis, from Late Latin *canapūceum; compare Italian canapuccio (“hempseed”). The development of -vui- to -vi- is regular, as also in vide.
Inherited from Old French chiere, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara (“face”), from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára). Compare Spanish cara.
Inherited from Old French chievrefeuil, from Late Latin caprifolium, from Latin caper + folium. Superficially it looks like a compound chèvre + feuille, but the gender is different.
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
Inherited from Late Latin caumāre (“to rest during the heat”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat”).

Inherited from Late Latin ministeriālis, from Latin ministerium. Doublet of ministériel.

parole.significato: metathesis (the breaking and reforming of double bonds in olefins in which substituent groups are swapped)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis).
Borrowed from Late Latin metempsychōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis).
Inherited from Late Latin mixtīcius, from Latin mixtus. Cognate with Portuguese mestiço, Spanish mestizo, Italian meticcio.

parole.significato: metonymy (use of a single characteristic or part of an object, concept or phenomenon to identify the entire object, con…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metonymia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin metōnymicus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μετωνυμικός (metōnumikós). By surface analysis, métonymie + -ique.
From Late Latin nātūrālitātem.
Inherited from Late Latin nigella, substantivization of the feminine of Latin nigellus (“blackish”).
Borrowed from Late Latin nigella. Doublet of nielle, which was inherited.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin nōtōrius.
Inherited from Middle French nourrisse, nourrice, from Old French nurrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, feminine of Latin nūtrīcius.

parole.significato: infant; baby; nursling (a child who breastfeeds)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin *nūtrītiōnem (distinct from the abstract noun nūtrītiō), from nūtrītus, past participle of nūtriō.

Inherited from Middle French novice, from Old French novice, borrowed from Late Latin novīcius, novīcia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”), from Latin novīcius, novītius (“new, newly arrived”), from novus (“new”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nūditās, from nūdus (whence nu).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin numerārius, from numerus (whence French nombre).
From Middle French nutritif < Old French nutritif < Late Latin nūtritīvus, from the participle stem of Latin nūtriō (“to suckle”).

Borrowed from Late Latin neomēnia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nephriticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek νεφριτικός (nephritikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin obligātōrius, from obligō (whence French obliger).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin obsequiae, alteration of Latin exsequiae.
From Late Latin ochra, from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “yellow”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).
Inherited from Middle French octroy, alteration of Old French otroi, from otroier (“to grant”), from Late Latin auctōrizāre.

Inherited from Middle French oyseau, from Old French oisel c. 1100, from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Compare Norman ouaîsé, Franco-Provençal usél. Compare also the French oie
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin omissiōnem, from Latin omittō. See omettre and -tion.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin unctuōsus, from Latin unctum.
Learned formation based on Late Latin undula, undulātus; corresponds to a Medieval Latin or New Latin undulatio.

parole.significato: to undulate, to ripple, to wave
parole.testo: Back-formation from ondulation; corresponds to a Medieval or later Latin undulo, undulare, from Late Latin undula, a diminutive of Latin unda (whence French onde).
Borrowed from Late Latin onomatopoeïa.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin optātīvus.
From Late Latin ōrificium.
From os + -eux, or Late Latin ossuōsus, from Latin os.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ossuārium (“charnel house”), from ossuārius (“of or for bones”), from Latin os (“bone”).
From Old French ovrer, Late Latin operō, operāre, from the deponent Classical Latin verb operor. Doublet of œuvrer (an analogical form created to avoid the confusion with ouvrir) and opérer.
From Late Latin oidium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
Borrowed from Late Latin palliāre (“to cover with a cloak”), from pallium.
Borrowed from Late Latin palpābilis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin palpebrālis, from palpebra (whence paupière).
From Middle French panarice, borrowed from Late Latin panāricium, an alteration of parōnychium (“whitlow”), influenced by panus (“tumor”).
Inherited from Old French parabole, borrowed from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parole, which was inherited.

parole.significato: paradigm (pattern, way of doing something; especially pattern of thought, system of beliefs, conceptual framework)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin paradīgma, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
Inherited from Old French parcelle, from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula. More-or-less a doublet of particule.
Inherited from Old French pardoner, from Late Latin perdōnāre.

Borrowed from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
Borrowed from Late Latin parentēla.
Borrowed from Late Latin paritātem.

From Old French, from paroisse + -al, corresponding to Late Latin parochiālis, from parochia.
Borrowed from Late Latin paronymon. By surface analysis, para- + -onyme.

From Middle French partial, borrowed from Late Latin partiālis (“relating to a part”), from Latin pars (“part”). Doublet of partiel.
Inherited from Old French parvis, parevis, from Late Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah. Doublet of paradis.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Byzantine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin patrimōniālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”).
From Late Latin patrōnātus.

parole.significato: land; region; home ground; homeland; home country; country; nation
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French pays, from Old French pais, from Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), derived from Latin pāgus (“countryside; district”). See related terms. Cognates include Italian paese. Borrowed into Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish as país. Cognates in regional language
Inherited from Old French peler, from Late Latin pilāre (“remove hair, depilate”), from Latin pilus, perhaps influenced by Old French pel.
Inherited from Old French pelice, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”).

Inherited from Old French pendre, from Late Latin pendĕre (conjugation confused with or altered by pendere (“to suspend, hang”)) for Latin pendēre, present active infinitive pendeō, from Proto-Italic *pendēō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).
Inherited from Old French pensif, from penser (“to think”), semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin pēnsō.
Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis (from Latin percipiō).
Inherited from Old French perdiciun, borrowed from Late Latin perditiōnem, from Latin perdō.
Borrowed from Late Latin permeābilis.
From Late Latin perplexitātem.

parole.significato: act of searching for someone or something
parole.testo: From Late Latin perquisitionem, from Latin perquirō.

parole.significato: blue-green (particularly used in reference to eyes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin persus (“Persian”).

parole.significato: personality, character (set of non-physical psychological and social qualities that make one person distinct from anoth…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin persōnālitās.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin persuāsīvus. Morphologically, from persuasion + -if.
From Late Latin pervinca, in vinca pervinca (“periwinkle”), apparently originally a magical formula. Traffic wardens are so called from the colour of their uniforms.
Inherited from Middle French pharaon.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin physiognomia.

parole.significato: to understand; to get, to catch on, to twig, to cotton on
parole.testo: Believed to be derived from an adjective meaning "caught", from Late Latin *pedicus, from Latin pedica (“snare, shackle, fetter”), and therefore doublet of piéger.
Inherited from Old French peon, from Late Latin pedōnem, derived from Latin ped- (“foot”). Doublet of péon, which was borrowed from Spanish peón.
Inherited from Late Latin pietōsus.
From Old French plaine, from Late Latin plāna (“planing tool”).
Inherited from Late Latin platessa. Cognate with Italian platessa.
Inherited from Old French plenier, plener, borrowed from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus.

parole.significato: point (the sharp tip of an object)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin puncta, from the feminine form of Latin punctus, perfect passive participle of pungō (“to prick”).
Inherited from Middle French poitevin, from Old French poitevin, from Late Latin pictāvīnus, from Pictāvus (“Poitou”), of Gaulish origin. Equivalent to Poitou + -in.
Borrowed from Late Latin polītīa (“state, government”), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).
From Old French pomel (“rounded knob”) (12th c.), diminutive of pom (“sword's hilt”), from Late Latin pomellum, from Latin pomum (“apple”).
Borrowing from Late Latin populātiōnem from Latin populus (“people”).
Inherited from Old French portour, from Late Latin portātōrem, from Latin portō. By surface analysis, porter + -eur.
From porte + -ier. From Old French portier, from Late Latin portārius (“porter, gatekeeper”), from Latin porta.
Borrowed from Late Latin pōtābilis, from Latin potō.

parole.significato: postern (back gate, back door, side entrance)
parole.testo: From Old French posterne, alteration of posterle, from Late Latin posterula (“back door”), from Latin posterus (“later”).

Inherited from Old French pouil, peouil, püil, from Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, from pēdis, from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-. The singular is a back-formation from the plural (see also genou with the same development).
Inherited from Old French poudre, poldre, from Late Latin pulvera, neuter plural based on Latin pulvis m, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”).
Inherited from Old French poulain, polain (“baby animal”), from a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin pullāmen, from Latin pullus (“animal young”).
Inherited from Middle French pour, from Old French por, pur, from Late Latin pōr, from Latin prō.

From Middle French, from Old French porchacier, from por- + chacier, from Late Latin captiāre (“to capture”), from Latin captāre.
Inherited from Late Latin pullicēnus. Compare Italian pulcino.
Inherited from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poēsia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prandiālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praestīgiōsus. By surface analysis, prestige + -(i)eux.
From Middle French preuve, from Old French prueve, preuve; synchronically derivable from the verb prouver. Possibly corresponds to Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.
Inherited from Middle French preux, from Old French preu, proz (“brave”), from Late Latin prōde (“profitable, useful”). Doublet of prou.
Inherited from Old French prime vere (“spring”), from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”). So-named because the flower blooms early in spring.

parole.significato: to price (fix a price according to market forces)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin pretiāre, pretiō (“to appraise”), from Latin pretium (“price”). Unrelated to pris, the past participle of prendre, although it might be remotivated in that way by contemporary French speakers.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin problēmaticus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”) (whence problème).
Borrowed from Late Latin proclāmātiōnem, from Latin proclāmō.
Derived from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from Latin prō- (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōdigālitās.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin productīvus, or formed from Latin productus with the suffix -if.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).
Inherited from Old French prolongation, borrowed from Late Latin prōlongātiō. By surface analysis, prolonger + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōmptitūdō. By surface analysis, prompt + -itude.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prōnōminālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin proprietārius.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin prosēlytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”).
Inherited from Old French protection, itself borrowed from Late Latin prōtectiō, prōtectiōnis (“a covering over”), from prōtegere (“to protect, cover in front”).

Inherited from Old French pro (“profit”), from Late Latin prōde (“profitable, useful”), from Latin prōdest (“is useful”), third-person singular of prōsum (“be useful”), after being reanalyzed as prōde est. Compare Catalan prou, where the form is widely used.
Borrowed from Late Latin provocātiōnem, from Latin provocō.
Borrowed from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Compare the popular Old French provende, provendre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praecautiō, from praecaveō.

Borrowed from Late Latin praedecessor.
Borrowed from Late Latin praelevāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praeludium.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin praesūmptuōsus, from Latin praesūmō (whence présumer).

Borrowed from Late Latin praeventiōnem, from Latin praeventus, from praevenio.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin praevisiō, from praevideō.
Borrowed from Late Latin pulpōsus, from Latin pulpa. By surface analysis, pulpe + -eux. Cf. the older form poulpeux.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pulverizāre, from Latin pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”) (whence French poudre).
Alteration of Old French purté, inherited from Late Latin pūritātem, from Latin pūrus (“pure”) + -tās (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, pur + -eté.
Inherited from Old French puree; feminine past participle of verb purer (“to make pure”), from Late Latin purare (same sense), from Classical Latin pūrus (“pure”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin putrefactiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French paste, from Old French paste, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
Borrowed from Late Latin peremptiōnem.

parole.significato: pericope (section of text forming a coherent thought)
parole.testo: From Late Latin pericope, from Greek περικοπή (perikopḗ, “section”).
Borrowed from Late Latin perinaeum, from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion).
Borrowed from Late Latin peritonaeum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin peraequātiō.
Inherited from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *pistrīre, *pistriō, a derivative of Latin pistor (“baker”).

Borrowed from Late Latin quadrumanus, from quattuor (whence French quatre) and manus (whence French main).
Inherited from Old French quarante, from Late Latin quarranta, from Vulgar Latin *quadrāntā, from Latin quadrāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”).
Inherited from Middle French quenoulle, from Old French quenoille, from Late Latin conucula, dissimilated form of colucula, from Latin colus.
Borrowed from Late Latin quaestiōnārius, from quaestiōnō, from Latin quaestiō.
From quinze + -ième, compare Late Latin quindecimus.
Borrowed from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus.
Inherited from Old French *raicine, from Late Latin rādīcīna (“root”), from Latin rādīx (“root”) + -īna (derivational suffix).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rādīcālis.
Inherited from Middle French rage, from Old French rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs.

parole.significato: to troat, cry, bellow, make noises
parole.testo: From Old French raire, from Late Latin ragĕre. Compare Romanian rage. Compare also railler.

Inherited from Old French resnable, from Late Latin ratiōnābilis, from Latin ratiō. Equivalent to raison + -able.
Inherited from Old French rasuir, from Late Latin rasōrium, from Latin rāsus (“shaved”). By surface analysis, raser + -oir.

From Old French rectifier, from Late Latin rectificāre (“rectify, regulate, control”).

From Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).
From Old French encontrer prefixed with re-, from Late Latin *incontrare.
Inherited from Old French rendre, from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere.
Inherited from Old French reposer, from Late Latin repausāre, from Latin pausāre.

parole.significato: to push back, push out of the way
parole.testo: From re- + pousser, or from Late Latin repulsāre.
From Late Latin restaurātōrem.
Borrowed from Late Latin restaurātiōnem. By surface analysis, restaurer + -ation.
Inherited from Middle French restriction, from Old French restriction, borrowed from Late Latin restrictiōnem, from Latin restringō.

parole.significato: rhubarb (any plant of the genus Rheum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin reubarbarum.
Borrowed from Late Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin rigōrōsus. By surface analysis, rigueur + -eux.
Inherited from Middle French rire, from Old French rire, from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. The past participle's root-final S was lost.

parole.significato: the quality of being laughable, risibility
parole.testo: From Late Latin rīsibilitās, itself from rīsibilis (“laughable”) + -tās (-ness, -ity). Equivalent to risible + -ité.

Inherited from Old French reont, from Late Latin retundus, dissimilated variant of Latin rotundus. Doublet of rotonde.

parole.significato: a landholding in New France, immediately below the level of seigneurie, and typically between 40 and 200 square arpents…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin ruptūra. Doublet of rupture.

Borrowed from Late Latin recompēnsāre, from Latin re + compenso.
Borrowed from Late Latin redhibitōrius, from redhibeō.
Inherited from Middle French real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs.

Borrowed from Late Latin reflexiōnem. By surface analysis, refléter + -xion.
From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regere (“rule”).

Inherited from Old French regulisse, ricolisse, metathesized form of licoresse (whence English licorice, liquorice), from Late Latin liquiritia, alteration of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza): γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”).
From régulier + -ité, or borrowed from Late Latin regularitātem.
Inherited from Old French reguler, borrowed from Late Latin regulāris.

Borrowed from Late Latin reservātiōnem, reservātiōnem, from Classical Latin reservātus, perfect passive participle of reservō.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin resolūbilis, from Latin resolvō.
Inherited from Old French resurrection, borrowed from Late Latin resurrēctiōnem.
From Old French restif, from Late Latin *restivus, from restare.

Inherited from Middle French sablon, from Old French sablon, sablun, from Late Latin sablō, sablōnem, from Latin sabulōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin salvātōrem.

parole.significato: sanatorium (institution that treats chronic diseases and provides supervised recuperation and convalescence)
parole.testo: From Late Latin sānātōrium (“giving health”) from Latin sānātus, past participle of sānō (“to cure, to heal”).
From Late Latin sānctificātiōnem.
From Old French saintuaire, from Late Latin and Latin sanctuārium (“sacred place, shrine”), from Latin sanctus (“holy, sacred”).
Inherited from Late Latin sanguilentus, alternative form of sanguinolentus (whence sanguinolent).
Borrowed from Late Latin sarcasmus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós).
Inherited from Late Latin sarculāre, derived from Latin sarculum.
Borrowed from Late Latin Saracēnī (plural), from Ancient Greek Σᾰρᾰκηνοί (Sărăkēnoí), most likely from Arabic.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin saturātiō. By surface analysis, saturer + -ation.
Inherited from Old French saucice, from Late Latin [farta] salsīcia, ultimately from Latin sāl (“salt”).
Inherited from Old French salmuire, from Late Latin salimuria, from Latin sal + muria.

Inherited from Middle French saulver, from Old French sauver, salver, from Gallo-Romance salvar, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus. In the sense specific to North America, a semantic loan from English save.
Inherited from Old French salveor, sauveor, from Late Latin salvātōrem. By surface analysis, sauver + -eur.
From saveur + -eux or Late Latin sapōrōsus, from Latin sapor.

parole.significato: Saxon (native or inhabitant of Saxony, Germany) (usually male)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French Saxon, borrowed from Late Latin Saxō, of West Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Sahsō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scabrōsus.

parole.significato: to scandalize, to cause a scandal
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandale + -iser.

Via Old French, from Late Latin scissiōnem, from Latin scindere.

Inherited from Late Latin sēminālia. By surface analysis, semer + -aille.

Inherited from Middle French sepmaine, from Old French semaine, from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”).

parole.significato: to seem, to resemble, to look like
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French sembler, from Old French sembler, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). Doublet of simuler.
Inherited from Old French semance, semence, from Late Latin sementia, plural of sementium, neuter form derived from Latin sēmentis, itself derived from sēmen (“seed”).
Borrowed from Late Latin sempiternālis.

parole.significato: soliloquy (act of a character speaking to himself)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin soliloquium.

Borrowed from Late Latin somnolentia, derived from Latin somnus (“sleep”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sorōricīdium.

Inherited from Old French, inherited from Late Latin soldus, from Latin solidus. Doublet of solide. See also the form sol, which kept the historical spelling from Old French, even if it came to be pronounced like sou.

parole.significato: shoe, boot (protective covering for the foot)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French soler, from Late Latin subtelāris.
From Middle French souppe, from Old French sope, supe, soupe, from Late Latin suppa (“sopped bread”), from Proto-Germanic *supô.
Borrowed from Late Latin subtractiōnem, and based on soustraire.
Borrowed from Late Latin spatula. Doublet of épaule, which was inherited.

parole.significato: spermatic (of, pertaining to, or resembling sperm)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin spermatĭcus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin sphinctēr (“the muscle of the anus”), from Ancient Greek σφῐγκτήρ (sphĭnktḗr, “lace, band; contractile muscle”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra. Replaced Old French espere, from the same Latin source.
Borrowed from Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna.
Borrowed from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spiritus.

parole.significato: spontaneous, self-generated (happening without any apparent external cause)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin spontāneus. In modern French, only words descending from Latin borrowings of Greek origin ending in the suffixes -ēus/-ēum, -aeus/-aeum (and exceptionally -ius/-ium, as in élysée/Élysée) are written with -ée in the masculine. Words descending from Latin words in -ān
Inherited from Old French speculatif, borrowed from Late Latin speculativus. By surface analysis, spéculer + -atif.
First attested circa 1350, borrowed from Late Latin speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor.
Inherited from Old French statut, from Late Latin statūtum (“a statute”), neuter singular of Latin statūtus, past participle of statuō (“to set up, establish”).
Borrowed from Late Latin stater, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στατήρ (statḗr).
Inherited from Middle French stupéfaction, borrowed from Late Latin stupefactiōnem, from Latin stupefaciōnem, from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) + faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: hem, border of a plate or cup
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French soue (“rope”) + -age, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin soca, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *soucā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati).
From Late Latin subalternus.
Borrowed from Late Latin subordinātiōnem. See also subordonner and -ation.
Borrowed from Late Latin substantiālis. By surface analysis, substance + -iel.
From Late Latin substantīvum, neuter singular of substantīvus (“substantive”), from substantia (“substance, essence”).
From Late Latin subventiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin subversiō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin superficiālis. By surface analysis, superficie + -el.
Borrowed from Late Latin superfluitātem. By surface analysis, superflu + -ité.

Inherited from Old French superlatif, borrowed from Late Latin superlātīvus, from Latin superlātus (“extravagant, of hyperbole”), past participle of superfero (“carry over”), from super (“above”) + fero (“bear, carry”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin supernumerārius, with substitution of prefix. By surface analysis, sur- + numéraire.
Borrowed from Late Latin susceptibilis.
Inherited from Middle French sympathic, from sympathie, from Late Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia), from συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin syndicus (“syndic”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate of a defendant”).

From syn- + -onyme, from Late Latin synonymon, from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), composed by σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Borrowed from Late Latin syntagma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύνταγμα (súntagma, “syntactical element”).
From Middle French sintaxe, borrowed from Late Latin syntaxis, from Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”).

Inherited from Middle French systeme (first attested 1552), from Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
From Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שֵׁם (šem)

parole.significato: sequence (set of things in a set order)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin sequentia, from Latin sequēns.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sēriōsus, from Classical Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”).
Inherited from Old French taillier, from Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”).
Inherited from Middle French tamis, from Old French tamis, from Late Latin tamisium, from Frankish *tamisu (“sieve, screen”). Cognate with English temse. Compare also regional Italian tamiso.
From Late Latin tinca.
Borrowed from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangō.

Inherited from Middle French taisnere, tesniere, derived from Old French taisson (“badger”), from Late Latin taxōnem, itself of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz (compare German Dachs (“badger”)).
Inherited from Old French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus.
Variant of tourte, from Late Latin torta.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin terminālis, from Latin terminus.
Back-formation from termites. From Late Latin termites (plural of termes), late variant of the Classical Latin tarmes (“woodworm”).

parole.significato: territorial (of, relating to or restricted to a specific geographic area, or territory)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin territoriālis, from Latin territorium. By surface analysis, territoire + -al.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin thesaurizāre, from Ancient Greek θησαυρίζω (thēsaurízō, “to store, treasure up”), from θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “store-room, treasure, granary, strong-box”).
Inherited from Late Latin tīmōnem, alteration of Classical Latin tēmōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin titulāris.
Borrowed from Late Latin tmēsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τμῆσις (tmêsis).
Inherited from Late Latin tōnsiōnem, from Latin tondeō (“shave, cut hair”).
Inherited from Middle French tumbe, tombe, from Old French tumbe, tombe, from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
Inherited from Middle French tumbeau, from Old French tumbel, tombel, diminutive of tumbe, from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos). By surface analysis, tombe + -eau.

parole.significato: to thunder, crack (make a sound like thunder)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin tonitruō, from tonitrus (“thunder”) (whence tonnerre).

parole.significato: torsion; act of turning or twisting
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French torsion, borrowed from Late Latin torsiōnem, from Latin tortiōnem.
Inherited from Late Latin tortūra, from Latin tortus, from torqueō.

Inherited from Old French turterele, turtrele, from Late Latin turturella or Latin turturilla, a diminutive of turtur (“turtle dove”). Compare Italian tortorella, Romanian turturea. Compare also tourte / tourtre.
Borrowed from Late Latin tractiōnem, from trahō.

Inherited from Middle French trembler, from Old French trambler, trembler, from Late Latin tremulāre, ultimately from Latin tremere (one of the sources of French craindre). Morphological doublet of trémuler.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin triangulāris. By surface analysis, triangle + -aire.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin tribulātiō, from Latin tribulō.
From Late Latin truella, from Latin trulla.

Inherited from Late Latin troia. Cognate with Italian troia, Occitan truèja, Catalan truja, Walloon troye. Further origin uncertain: * It has been compared to Latin porcus Troiānus (literally “Trojan pig”), a singularly attested name for a stuffed roast of pork, so called by humorous comparison to t
From Old French, from Late Latin tructa, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs).

parole.significato: trestle (a folding or fixed set of legs used to support a table-top or planks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French trestel, inherited from Late Latin trānstellum, diminutive of Latin trānstrum beam.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin tyrannia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννία (turannía). By surface analysis, tyran + -ie.
Inherited from Old French unifier, borrowed from Late Latin unificare.
Inherited from Old French union, borrowed from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ūnivocus.
Borrowed from Late Latin urgentem, present participle of urgeō.
Borrowed from Late Latin ūrēthra, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūsūrpātor. By surface analysis, usurper + -ateur.
Unadapted borrowing from Late Latin ūvula (“small grape”), diminutive of Latin ūva. Doublet of uvule, another borrowing.
Borrowed from Late Latin ūvula (“small grape”), diminutive of Latin ūva. Doublet of uvula.
Borrowed from Late Latin vagābundus.

Inherited from Middle French vaisseau, from Old French vaissel, from Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of Latin vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vessel”). Compare Occitan vaissèl, Catalan vaixell, Italian vascello.
Inherited from Old French valur, valeur, valor, from Late Latin valōrem, accusative singular form of valor, from Latin valeō.

Inherited from Middle French vandoise, from Old French vendoise, from Late Latin *vindēsia, *vindisia, from Gaulish *wind-ēsyā, from Proto-Celtic *windos (“white”) + a nominal suffix -ēsyā. Cognate with English vendace (“types of whitefish”), Norman vendeise, and Walloon vindwesse.
Inherited from Old French veelle, from Late Latin vitella, diminutive of Latin vitula.
From velours. See also velu (“hairy”), inherited from Late Latin villūtus, ultimately from Latin villus (“hair, tuft of hair”). Cognate with English velvet.
Inherited from Late Latin villūtus, derived from Latin villus (“tuft, hair”).
Inherited from Old French vengeor, vengeour, vengedur. By surface analysis, venger + -eur. Possibly corresponding to Late Latin vindicātōrem, from Latin vindicō. Compare Spanish vengador.

parole.significato: ventilation: replacement of stale or noxious air with fresh
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ventilātiōnem, from Latin ventilō.
Borrowed from Late Latin verbālis. By surface analysis, verbe + -al.
From Middle French verbosité, borrowed from Late Latin verbōsitās. By surface analysis, verbeux + -ité.
From the Late Latin verna, from Gaulish *werna, from Proto-Celtic *wernā (“alder”). Compare Old Irish fern.

Inherited from Middle French verd, vert, from Old French vert, from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish verde. The Old French -t is due to regular final devoicing. The feminine was originally also vert and was extended with -e only dur
Learned borrowing from Late Latin verticālis.

Probably from Late Latin verva, a variant of Latin verba (“words; discourse; expressions; language”), the plural of verbum (“word”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wérdʰom (“that which is said; utterance, word”), from the verb *wérdʰeti (“to speak, say”), derived from the root *werh₁- + *-dʰet
Borrowed from Late Latin vesperālis.
From Middle French vieulx, from Old French viel, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
Inherited from Old French vilain, vilein, villein, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from Latin vīlla. Not related to vil.
Borrowed from Late Latin virulentus. The second sense is probably a semantic loan from English.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin viscerālis. By surface analysis, viscère + -al.
Inherited from Middle French viser, from Old French viser, from Late Latin vīsāre, from Latin vīsere, intensive of videō. Compare voir.
Inherited from Middle French visqueux, from Old French viscous, borrowed from Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum.
Borrowed from Late Latin vocābulārium, from Latin vocabulum.
Inherited from Old French voisin, veisin, from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.
Inherited from Old French volille, volleille, from Late Latin volātilia, from Latin volātilis. Doublet of volatil.
Borrowed from Late Latin volūminōsus, from volūmen (whence volume).
From Old French voer, vuer, from Late Latin vōtāre, denominal from vōtum; or simply formed from vœu + -er. Doublet of voter (from English). Compare also Italian votare, Spanish and Portuguese votar.
Borrowed from Late Latin vulnerābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin veniālis, from Latin venia.
Borrowed from Late Latin venēnōsus. More or less a doublet of venimeux.

parole.significato: cylinder (the space in which a piston travels inside a reciprocating engine or pump)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin veruina (“long javelin”), from Latin veru (“javelin”).
From Middle French ere, here (16th c.), a borrowing from Late Latin aera.
Borrowed from Late Latin ēbullitiōnem.

parole.significato: scaffold (elevated platform on which a criminal is executed)
parole.testo: Alteration of Old French chafaud, from Late Latin *catafalicum, from Ancient Greek κατά- (katá-) + Latin fala (“tower”). Doublet of catafalque.
Inherited from Old French eschauder, eschalder, from Late Latin excaldāre, a verb based on Latin caldus (“hot”), from earlier calidus.

From past participle of échoir + -ance, possibly, but less likely, corresponding to a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *excadentia, from *excadens from *excadere, from Latin cadere (“fall”). Compare Italian scadenza.
From Late Latin *exclaricire, from Latin claricare.
From Old French escluse, from Late Latin exclūsa [aqua], from the classical Latin verb exclūdō, exclūdere.

parole.significato: (university) student, scholar (especially in the Middle Ages)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French escolier, escoler, an early borrowing from Late Latin scholāris (equivalent to école + -ier), from Latin schola. Compare also the doublet scolaire, a later borrowing.

parole.significato: to skin (to remove the skin off)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French escorchier, inherited from Late Latin excorticāre, from cortex. Compare the borrowing décortiquer and Catalan escorxar. Distantly related to écorcer.

parole.significato: to shorten, curtail (make shorter e.g. by cutting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French escurter, from Late Latin excurtāre, from Latin curtāre. By surface analysis, é- + court + -er.
Inherited from Late Latin scrīptōrium, or possibly formed in French, from écrit + -oire.

Inherited from Middle French escureul, escuirel, escurel, from Old French escurel from Late Latin *scūriolus, diminutive of *scūrius, variant of Classical Latin sciūrus, from Ancient Greek σκίουρος (skíouros).
Inherited from Middle French escuyer, from Old French escuier, inherited from Late Latin scūtārius. Doublet of scutaire.

Inherited from Old French letuaire, respelled to more closely match Late Latin ēlectuārium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”), from ἐκλείχω (ekleíkhō, “to lick up”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēligibilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin elongātiōnem.

parole.significato: lucubration, elucubration (results of intense study with little value; used ironically)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēlūcubrātiō, from ēlūcubrō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elegīacus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin epanalēpsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπανάληψις (epanálēpsis).

parole.significato: spelt (Triticum aestivum subsp. spelta or Triticum spelta)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French, from Old French espiautre, espelte (“spelt, corn”), from Late Latin spelta (“spelt”).
Borrowed from Late Latin epilēpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληπτικός (epilēptikós).
Inherited from Old French epistre, epistle, from Late Latin epistola (probably a semi-learned borrowing), from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ). Doublet of épistule / épistole.
Borrowed from Late Latin aequidistantem.
Borrowed from Late Latin aequivocus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ērūctātiō. By surface analysis, éructer + -ation.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin erēmīticus, from Latin erēmīta (whence French ermite).
From Middle French estappe, from Old French estaple, from Middle Dutch stapel, from Old Dutch stapul, from Frankish *stapul.
Probably from a dialectal variant of éteule (“stubble”) + -er, from Old French esteule, dialectal variant of Picard estoble, from Late Latin stupula, from Latin stipula (“stubble, stalk”).
From Middle French estoile, from Old French estoile, esteile, from Late Latin stēla, from Latin stēlla. Doublet of Estelle.
From Old French esturnel, from Late Latin sturnellus, from Latin sturnus.

Inherited from Middle French étront, from Old French estront, from Late Latin struntus, borrowed from Frankish *strunt, from Proto-Germanic *strunt- (“stump”), from *strent- (“to be stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“stiff”). Compare Italian stronzo (“asshole, dumbass”), Dutch stront (“fec
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ēvangelizāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin evictiōnem, from Latin evincō.
From évêque + -é (suffix forming abstract nouns), or from Late Latin or Ecclesiastical Latin epīscopātus.
Inherited from Old French evesque, inherited from Late Latin episcopus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos).
From Late Latin iambicus.
Borrowed from Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).
Most likely from a- + long + -er, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre, from Latin longus.

Inherited from Middle French aveugle from Old French avogle, from Late Latin ab oculīs (“without eyes”, literally “away from the eyes”), possibly a calque of Ancient Greek ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων (apò ommátōn) or more likely from Gaulish exops. The current French form is either an exception to the normal sound
Either from Late Latin *baga (“a vessel type”), or from Old French bague (“pack, bundle”); ultimately from the North Germanic/Scandinavian source (Old Norse baggi) that yielded English bag.

Of uncertain origin: possibly from Late Latin *bifĭlis, *bifīlis (“double wire”), from Latin bĭfīlum, composed of bis (“twice”) + filum (“fiber”). Inherited from Old French baston, probably from a Vulgar Latin bastōnem, itself a modification of Late Latin bastum, or possibly noun use of the verb *bastāre, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō). Compare Italian bastone.

parole.significato: a fleshy pinkish color (not the color of a carnation flower)
parole.testo: From Middle French, possibly from Italian carnagione (“flesh color”), either way from Late Latin carnātiōnem (“fleshiness”) (from Latin carō (“flesh”)), or from a corruption of coronation (from Latin corōnāre (“to crown”), from corōna (“crown”)), because of the flower's use in chaplets or from the t

parole.significato: a wooden basket, bin or chest in which dairy products such as cheese and butter were stored in the past
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French chasier, casier (“wicker basket in which cheese was left to dry”), formed as a masculine derivative of chasiere, casiere, itself from an abbreviation of a syntagma involving Latin forma (“form”), cratis (“wickerwork”), cista (“trunk, chest, casket”), or sporta (“basket, ham
From cercle + -er, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *circlāre, from Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī (and therefore a doublet of the borrowed circuler). Compare Italian cerchiare.

parole.significato: a path, way, route, or road, large enough to fit carriages, chariots, carts, wagons, etc.
parole.testo: From char + -ière, or from Late Latin (via) carrāria, from Latin carrus. Doublet of carrière (“career”), taken from Old Occitan. Compare Occitan carrièra, Catalan and Spanish carrera, Portuguese carreira, archaic Italian carraia, Romanian cărare.
Inherited from Old French crestiente, from Late Latin Christiānitātem (“Christianity”), from Latin Christianus. Or from chrétien + -té, based on the Latin word.
From ciment + -ier or from Late Latin caementārius, from Latin caementum.

parole.significato: to nail (to attach using a nail)
parole.testo: From clou (“nail”), or alternatively from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus. Compare Italian chiavare, Catalan clavar.

Inherited from Middle French compaignie, from Old French compaignie, from compain + -ie or alternatively from compagne, from Vulgar Latin *compania, from Late Latin compāniō, from Latin cum + pānis (“bread”). See also copain, compagnon.
Either from conjecture + -er or from Late Latin coniectūrō, coniectūrāre, from Latin coniectūrus, future active participle of cōniciō (“to throw or bring together, unite, connect”).

Inherited from Middle French corbeau m, from Old French corbel m, itself either a diminutive of corp m (“raven”), or from a Late Latin corbellus, corvellus m, from Latin corvus m (Vulgar Latin variant *corbus m).
Uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin crosuin, from Latin corrosum, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *crosus, of Gaulish origin.

Alteration of Old French duel, plural dueus (possibly influenced by analogy to œil and its plural), which probably came from Late Latin dolus, a derivative of Latin dolor (“pain”), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dolium, from cordolium.
Inherited from Old French deschaucier. By surface analysis, dé- + chausser. Or from Late Latin discalceāre, from Latin calceāre.

Inherited from Old French deschauz, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of Late Latin discalceātus, from discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. parole.significato: to lunch, to eat lunch, to have lunch
parole.testo: From dé- + jeûner (“un fast (to break fast)”) or from a Vulgar Latin *disieiūnāre, from Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare Catalan dejunar, Spanish desayunar, Italian digiunare, Occitan dejunar, Portuguese desjejuar. Doublet of dîner from which English dine descended.
Inherited from Middle French departir, from Old French departir, from Late Latin departīre, from Latin de + partiō. Or from dé- + partir.

Inherited from Middle French desployer, from Old French desploier, desploiier, itself from a compound of des- and ploiier, or possibly from Late Latin displicāre, or from Latin dēplicāre (“to unfold”).

parole.significato: to nail in, put a nail in
parole.testo: From Old French encloer. By surface analysis, en- + clou + -er. Or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre, from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus.
Inherited from Old French englotir, from Late Latin ingluttīre, from Latin gluttiō; alternatively, from Old French en- + glotir.

Inherited from Middle French escallier, borrowed (through written form) from Occitan escalier, from Late Latin scālārium (attested in some inscriptions), neuter nominalization of *scālārius (“pertaining to a flight of stairs”), or from scālāris, from Latin scāla (“ladder”). Replaced the older French

parole.significato: to clad in iron (transitive), to be clad in iron (intransitive)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French [Term?], from fer, or from Late Latin ferrāre (cf. classical ferrātus), from Latin ferrum. Compare Catalan and Portuguese ferrar; Italian ferrare; Spanish herrar.
Inherited from Late Latin frīgorōsus, from Latin frīgus, or from a Vulgar Latin *frigidulōsus (contracted to *fridlōsus), from frigidus. Compare Romanian friguros.

Inherited from Middle French garser (“to skin, flay”), from Old French garser, jarser (“to gash, wound”), possibly from Late Latin caraxāre, charaxāre, from Ancient Greek χαράσσειν (kharássein, “to cut, incise”). Alternatively from Latin *carptiāre, from carpĕre (“to pull, pluck”). Cognate with Gali

Inherited from Old French jugement. By surface analysis, juger + -ment. Or from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō (“to pass judgement upon”). Compare Occitan and Catalan jutjament; Old Italian giudicamento; Spanish juzgamiento; Portuguese julgamento.
From laine + -ier (Old French lanier) or possibly from Late Latin lānārius, from Latin lāna.

Inherited from Middle French limignon, lumignon, from Old French limeignons (“candle-wick”), eventually from Late Latin licinium, from ellychnium (“lamp-wick”), from Ancient Greek ἐλλύχνιον (ellúkhnion, “lamp-wick”). The intermediate forms perhaps received influence from Medieval Latin lūminiōnem (“

Inherited from Old French manevele, probably from a Vulgar Latin *manabella, alteration of *manibula, variant of Latin manicula (and therefore a doublet of manicle), from manus (“hand”), or alternatively from Late Latin manuālis.

Inherited from Middle French marteau m, from a back-formation from Old French marteaus (ca. 1140), plural of martel, from Late Latin martellus, from martulus, variant form of marculus, diminutive of Latin marcus, or from malleus.

From an alteration of Old French moitoier, moitoieor, moitieur, from Late Latin medietārius, from Latin medius (“middle, half”). Or alternatively from moitié + -ier. See also Italian mezzadro, Spanish mediero.

parole.significato: stone (of a fruit), pit (of a fruit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French noyau, backformed from Old French noiaus, plural of noial, a variant of Old French noel, from either Early Medieval Latin nōdellus (“buckle”), diminutive of nōdus (“knot”), or Late Latin nucālis (“nut-like”), derivative of nux (“nut”). Compare English newel and noil.

parole.significato: straw house (a building to store straw)
parole.testo: From Latin paleārium, or from Late Latin paleāre, from paleāris.

From Old French pichier, bichier (compare English pitcher), from Late Latin pīcārium, bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Compare Italian bicchiere, German Becher.

parole.significato: to discharge somebody from an obligation
